idiom_name: no realization - the libuv event loop is the permanent single leader
alternative: async/await over the loop's built-in non-blocking I/O; worker_threads for CPU-bound work only; cluster (primary accepts and hands sockets to workers) or process-per-core for multi-core scaling - never a hand-written shared-handle thread pool
implementation_notes: Node's runtime contradicts the pattern's premise rather than merely lacking a helper. libuv's design documentation states that a loop "is meant to be tied to a single thread", that the loop and its handles are "not thread-safe", and that network I/O is "always performed in a single thread, each loop's thread": the demultiplexing leader is the loop's thread and cannot be rotated, and a listening socket belongs to one loop. Threads exist but are the wrong instrument: the worker_threads documentation says workers "do not help much with I/O-intensive work" because the built-in asynchronous I/O is more efficient. Spread accepts across processes with cluster, where the primary accepts and distributes sockets, rather than trying to share handles between threads.
pitfalls: Synchronous work (readFileSync, pbkdf2Sync, a long loop) blocks the loop's thread and with it every socket it demultiplexes - no other thread can take over the leader role.
Handles cannot be shared between worker threads; messages and transferable/shared ArrayBuffers are the only cross-thread channels, so a shared handle set is not expressible.
cluster is not a thread pool: the primary accepts and distributes connections (an acceptor/connector arrangement) and workers are separate processes with no shared in-memory state.
Using worker_threads for I/O work duplicates the loop and adds serialization overhead without improving throughput.
